items.content:
What should scare Maintenance leaders more: AI watching motor drift, or finding out after the line is already down?

Start with stability.

That’s where AI belongs in Maintenance first.

On the machine.
On the motor.
On the bearing.
On the press brake that always sounds “a little different,” until it finally stops the line.

IoT sensors can read vibration, temperature, current, pressure, cycle drift, and motor behavior before the machine fails.

AI connects those signals:

- A bearing runs hotter.
- A motor pulls more current.
- A cycle drifts from normal.
- A vibration pattern changes.

Alone, each signal may look small.

Together, they say:

“This asset is moving away from stable condition.”

Now imagine the Maintenance Manager at the end of the shift.

He gets a WhatsApp alert:

Press brake #4
20% probability of bearing failure within 5 days.
Vibration trend rising.
Current draw unstable.
Inspect during the next planned window.

The machine hasn’t failed yet.
The line hasn’t stopped yet.
Nobody is running around looking for parts.

The system gave the team time.

Time to inspect.
Time to plan.
Time to fix the issue before it becomes another emergency.

That’s the real value of AI in Maintenance.

It turns weak signals into visible risk.

It turns “something feels off” into a clear action.

Start with one critical asset.

Ask one question:

Where do we usually find out too late?
That’s where AI should start.

A lot of factories say they have pull.

They have boards.
Cards.
Signals.

But the floor still behaves like push.

Jobs are released too early.
WIP keeps growing between operations.
Supervisors keep expediting.

The bottleneck is buried before anyone admits it.

Then AI shows up.

It reads the drift.

The queue between step 2 and step 3.
The orders released without material.
The jobs started before tooling was ready.
The customer demand that changed 3 days ago.
The bottleneck everyone works around but no one protects.

That’s when the fear starts.

Because AI doesn’t just make the system faster.

It makes the hidden system visible.

If your Push system is creating inventory, AI will show it.
If your Pull system is fake, AI will show it.
If your schedule is flooding the floor, AI will show it.

And if the Pull system is real?

AI can strengthen it.

It can flag WIP before it turns into chaos.
Adjust kanban levels based on real usage.
Protect the bottleneck.
Check if a job is actually ready to release.
Read demand signals before yesterday’s forecast causes tomorrow’s fire.

The question is simple:

Are you using AI to make better decisions?

Or are you about to find out your “Pull system” was just Push with labels?

The floor tells the truth...
AI just makes it harder to ignore.

Posting every day is bullshit.

Here's why:

I see LinkedIn coaches telling their clients to post daily, minimum five times a week, if they want their account to grow.

That makes your content calendar look productive. 
But frequency without clarity is just noise.

Posting every day doesn't work unless you know:

- Who you actually want to talk to
- What problem keeps them up at 3am
- Why they'd choose you over the 50 other people in their feed

I know a lot of top creators post every day.

But that's because it's their job or they have a ghostwriter doing it for them.

If you're a founder without that luxury, focus on making sure every post has a purpose.

If you want leads and authority and to be the only person your ICP thinks of when they have the problem you solve.

Then you need to know exactly who you're talking to before you write a single word.

Know the pain.
Know the objection.
Know what makes them stop scrolling.

Consistency matters. 
I’m not saying it doesn’t of course it does. 

But consistency without knowing who your audience is pointless.

That's why when I coach people, I never say you have to post X amounts per week.

I ask: how many times can you realistically post a week while still providing real value for [insert target audience].

If that's every day, go for it…

But I need at least one day off. 


What’s one piece of LinkedIn advice you followed that never worked?

items.content:
Most predictive maintenance projects in mid-size shops follow the same arc. Sensors get installed. Dashboards get built. Alerts fire. 18 months later, nothing on the floor runs differently.

Ten failure modes I keep seeing. Almost never the model.

1. No standard work, no baseline to predict from. A model needs to know what "normal" looks like. If two operators run it two ways, the baseline is fiction. The prediction looks confident anyway.

2. Sensor data without process context. Vibration spike at 03:14. Was the machine cutting, idling, or in test mode? The sensor doesn't know. Neither does the model. The alert fires regardless.

3. Digital twin drifts, nobody validates. Built six months ago. The line has changed - new fixture, new feed rate, swapped servo. Decisions get made against a snapshot the floor has already walked past.

4. Model trained on bearing X, deployed on bearing Y. Maintenance swapped the part. Different vibration signature, different failure curve. The model was never retrained. It predicts failures that can't happen and misses the ones that can.

5. No feedback loop. The fix never returns to the model. Technician replaces the seal. The machine runs fine for nine months. That's the most valuable data the model could get. It stays in a notebook in someone's truck.

6. Tribal knowledge walks out the door. Lost a press brake operator last year. He was also the die maker. A drawer full of custom small dies - he knew which one was for which job because he'd made them. The day he left, the toolbox became a guessing game. No graph captured that.

7. Knowledge graph populated once, then abandoned. A consultant ran a workshop. Filled the schema. Got paid. Machines kept changing. The graph stayed frozen. Two years on, it documents a plant that no longer exists.

8. Alert into a vacuum. Dashboard wired into a shared Slack channel. The channel had no owner. The operator who saw the alert wasn't trained for it. By the time anyone figured out the next move, the bearing was gone. The alert worked as designed. The receiving end was never built.

9. Prediction without authority to act. The system says shut down for inspection. The plant manager has a shipment due Friday. Production wins. The prediction becomes a record of an action that didn't happen.

10. Reactive culture eats the predictive tool. Bonuses get paid for fixing things fast. Preventing the breakdown pays nothing. Operators learn what the org actually rewards.

Every one of these is a workflow problem in tech-shaped packaging. The standard. The context. The owner. The authority. The loop back. The incentive. AI amplifies what's already there - when the workflow's missing, it amplifies the absence.

Without standard work, AI only accelerates chaos. Before you automate the work, understand the work

items.content:
Can a part pass inspection and still be a defect?

Yes...

A part can be inside the tolerance and still miss the target.

That’s the uncomfortable lesson behind Genichi Taguchi’s quality thinking.
Most quality systems ask:

“Is it in spec?” - Useful question.

But not enough.

The better question is:

“How far is it from nominal?” - Because the customer doesn’t feel your tolerance chart.

They feel the fit.
They feel the noise.
They feel the assembly issue.
They feel the rework that shows up 3 operations later.

A part sitting at the edge of tolerance may pass inspection.

But it’s already telling you something.

The process is drifting.
Variation is too wide.
The system is accepting loss because the part is still “good enough.”

That’s where Aristotle connects to the floor.

Excellence isn’t one good part.

It’s the habit of hitting the target so often that variation starts to shrink.

Same principle, different century:

→ Every deviation carries a cost.
→ On-target beats barely in-spec.
→ Variation is the real signal.
→ Habits set the mean.
→ Quality starts before inspection.

Most operations still reward “inside the limit.”

The best ones chase the target.

Ask your floor this week:

Do you measure parts against the limit, or against the target?

Hit the target.
Shrink variation.
Cut the loss.

It gives Lean a training ground.

I gained 63K LinkedIn followers in 18 months. 

These are the exact systems I used:

(No gatekeeping or over-complicating things). 

The Profile Audit:

✔️ Profile picture = high quality and 80% face
✔️ Headline = tell your audience what you do
✔️ Banner = proof + CTA with one offer
✔️ About = your story, their pain, solution, next steps
✔️ Featured = single path to your offers

The 60-minute daily loop:

→ 15 mins warming the feed pre-posting
→ 15 mins to ship one new post
→ 15 mins replying to comments after posting

Half my feed says AI is going to collapse lean manufacturing...

I don’t buy it....

The Toyota House has held for 70 years and it still is the right structure.

Stability.
Just-in-Time.
Jidoka.
Standard work.
Kaizen.
Flow.

AI doesn’t remove those layers.

It puts new sensors, cameras, advisors, and feedback loops inside them.

Start with stability.

IoT sensors can read vibration, temperature, current, pressure, cycle drift, and motor behavior before the machine stops the line.
That turns maintenance from “call someone when it breaks” into... “this asset is drifting, check it before Friday.”

Same house.
Stronger foundation.

Now look at Jidoka...

A smart camera reads the station and the flow through it. Not just the person. The process itself.

After a while, people stop performing for the camera. You get closer to real behavior.

Then you define what value-added work looks like.

The camera classifies motion, waiting, walking, searching, rework, handoffs, and downtime against that definition.

At the end of the shift, the plant manager gets:
“Station#15. 17% NVA activity - Kaizen needed.”

Science fiction?

I don’t think so...

The pieces already exist. The hard work is defining VA and NVA clearly enough that the number means something.

Same with 5S.

A camera can take dozens of frames per minute at a workstation...

- Tools missing.
- Bins out of place.
- Material outside the marked zone.
- Shadow board gaps.
- Blocked aisle.

The 5S audit stops being a monthly theater exercise and becomes a live condition.

Then come the advisors.

A supervisor asks a SOP advisor how to handle a setup issue.
A lead asks a safety advisor what to check before restarting a cell.
HR answers policy questions without pulling the plant manager into every small issue.
A business advisor helps connect today’s floor problem with cost, lead time, and customer risk.

Even the brake operator starts using plain language with the press brake...
- “What bend sequence should I check first?”
- “Why is this program throwing an error?”
- “What changed from the last job?”

That’s where this gets real.

AI won’t save a chaotic floor.

It will just make chaos move faster.

But on top of clear standards, stable flow, and visible problems, AI becomes another layer of the operating system.

The technology is coming.

The question is simple:

Will we bolt it onto broken processes, or will we finally define the system clearly enough for AI to help?

Where would you start first?

Smart cameras for VA/NVA?
IoT sensors for preventive maintenance?
5S vision checks?
Supervisor AI advisors?

items.content:
A lot of plants learn lean backwards.

They start with what's visible. 5S. Kanban. OEE. Boards. Events. Labels. Tools.
Then the floor does what the floor always does.

The board gets ignored by Tuesday. The standard gets bypassed when orders run late. The hero fixes the same problem nobody wrote down. The schedule pushes work that creates rework before production starts. The OEE number looks fine while flow gets worse.

This visual collects 10 of those moments. Most plants will recognize at least half.

The pattern under all of them is one fact: a tool only works when the behavior around it is managed every day.

I learned this from a supervisor named Fausto. The sandwich station was running low on glue. The next bucket was a five-minute walk away. The old way: operators run out, stop, search, lose twenty minutes, nobody calls it a problem. The new way: Fausto saw it coming, walked the glue over before it ran out. The line never paused. Nobody noticed.

That's the whole job. Watch the flow. Remove friction before it stops the line.

Fausto left the plant five years after me. After him, lead times drifted back to three weeks. Same layout. Same tools. No one left to watch the flow.

These aren't tool failures. They're behavior gaps the tools were supposed to close.

If a tool doesn't change what happens on Tuesday afternoon, it's decoration.

Less heroics. More system.
Stability first. Everything else follows.
The floor tells the truth.

items.content:
Years ago I watched a Salvagnini laser go down on the floor. The cutting head had been failing for weeks. Burrs on edges, inconsistent pierce, sparks where there shouldn't be sparks. Operator flagged it twice. Nobody connected the dots until the part broke entirely. Replacement flew overnight from Italy. The downtime plus the courier added up to an embarrassing number.

What I keep coming back to: every signal that mattered was already in the machine. It just wasn't going anywhere useful.

Here's what a modern AI-driven PdM flow does with that same machine today.
1. Sensor on the cutting head captures capacitive feedback, gas flow, focal stability, every 100ms. Most of the stream is noise. The signal lives in patterns across many readings.

2. Signal processing converts the raw stream into FFT and trend curves. A capacitive drift invisible to a human in a week shows up as a clean diagonal on the chart.

3. Digital Twin runs a physics-based replica of the machine in parallel. Material, stress, optical path geometry, all modeled and compared to actual output in real time.

4. The Twin also generates synthetic failures to train the model on rare events. Cutting head focal drift, capacitive sensor noise, lens contamination, modeled before they happen on the floor.

5. Knowledge graph holds the domain knowledge in queryable form. Service manuals, failure history, manufacturer notes: a relationship graph the agent reads directly.

6. Reasoning engine with an LLM (DeepSeek or similar) runs root cause analysis. The output reads: "capacitive sensor on cutting head, progressive drift over 18 days, 73% confidence." Actionable, scoped, dated.

7. RAG pulls a specific manual fragment for the LLM at diagnosis time. Salvagnini's cutting head service section gets injected into the prompt context.

8. Action planner assigns a concrete task with priority and deadline. Output: "Order replacement cutting head, Salvagnini Italy, 3-week lead, install during week 14 changeover." A task with a slot, an owner, a deadline.

9. The outcome of every action feeds back into the Learning Module. The model misjudges the same machine less next time.

10. The whole loop closes from machine through diagnosis to action and back to machine. The architecture is the loop.

None of this is futuristic. Every signal in that Salvagnini story was already in the machine in 2018. The architecture above captures those signals and turns them into a task someone can act on.

Old way: one overnight flight from Italy. New way: a part ordered three weeks early, by normal courier.

AI does not fix broken operations. It amplifies what already exists. Before you automate the work, understand the work.

Waste in services rarely starts as “waste.”

It usually starts much earlier.

A few calls arrive unevenly.
One person becomes overloaded.
The team starts covering gaps.
Small delays turn into extra follow-ups.
Extra follow-ups create more emails, more meetings, more stress.
And before long, the system starts to snowball.

In manufacturing, we often talk about Muda — the 7 wastes.
But in service environments, I believe we need to look first at Mura and Muri:

Mura — unevenness
Muri — overburden
Muda — visible waste

Because waste is often not the root cause.
It is the result.

When workload is uneven, people compensate.
When people compensate too long, they burn out.
When they burn out, customers feel it.

The first question should not be:
“How do we make people work faster?”

The better question is:
“Where is the unevenness in the system?”

Fix the flow first.
Reduce the overburden.
Then the waste becomes much easier to see - and much easier to remove.

No drama.
Better facts.
Better flow.

What I notice most about how Western lean adopted Toyota's system is what got left at the dock.

This receiving report says more than any audit.

We imported the magnifying glass. We left the Mura sequence behind. We imported the kanban card. We left the diagnostic pile behind. We imported the andon cord. We left the positive signal behind. We imported the stopwatch. We left the standard WIP behind.

On the floor, this shows up in small ways.

The 5S board is laminated. Nobody knows why it's there. The kanban card moves. Nobody reads what it's saying. The andon light blinks. Nobody counts the pulls as wins. The SMED stopwatch runs. The changeover math never gets done.

The tools arrived. The structure got left at customs.

Lean is not a toolbox we adopted. It is a management system we copied parts of.

What good looks like sits one layer below the tool. Team leaders write the standard and own it. Andon pulls get counted as healthy signals all shift long. 5 Whys branches at every level until the cause is real. Pull lives in nesting math and changeover capability. items.content:
LinkedIn just shadow-banned one of my posts for absolutely no reason.

I posted 2 hours ago about how to grow on LinkedIn.

After one hour it had:

- 11 likes
- 15 comments
- 109 impressions

Normally my posts have 50-100 likes by that time. 

The even weirder part...

I posted almost the exact same thing 3 months ago.

That post went viral. 

106K impressions, 1,500+ engagements and 525 new followers.

Same content but completely different result.

I'm not posting this to complain because I don't tie my self-worth to likes (fortunately). 

But to show the LinkedIn algo punishes everyone, for absolutely no reason. 

It's not personal. 

LinkedIn make it make sense :/ 


Has anyone else experienced this recently?

P.S. I refuse to delete my LinkedIn post so this ugly monster is staying.
